text: Κατὰ τὴν θέσει κίνησιν. Sic etiam quæst. 56 Ad Thalass. Non satis Picus, in peragendo motu. Reddidi, voluntatis motu, non quod θελήσει velim emendatum, sed quod id, quod sic θέσει, quasi ab extrinseco et factitie est, voluntate est, at in adoptione, qua quis θέσει, non φύσει, in familiam filiumque cooptatur. Sic corpus ad animum effertur, ejus quasi ratione imbutum, qua voluntate virtutibus excolitur, supra illius, ut corpus est, meritum atque debitum.
anchorLine: τῷ νοῒ τὸ σῶμα κατὰ τὴν θέσει κίνησιν (u)· ἡ δὲ,
en: On 'by positional motion' (κατὰ τὴν θέσει κίνησιν). So also in Question 56 to Thalassius. Picus ('in peragendo motu') does not render it adequately. I have rendered it 'by a motion of the will', not because I would emend it to θελήσει ('by willing'), but because what is thus 'by position' (θέσει) is as if from outside and artificial, and is by will, as in adoption, by which one is taken into a family and made a son by position, not by nature. So the body is carried up to the mind, endued as it were with the mind's reason, by which it is cultivated by the will in virtues, above its own merit and due (as a body).

anchorLine: δρύνει καὶ τοῖς γνωρίσμασι ** · καὶ ἡ μὲν Παλαιὰ,
en: In Thalassius the reading is χαρίσμασι (a variant for the printed γνωρίσμασι).

text: Τῆς ἀληθοῦς θεουργίας. Veram θεουργίαν, seu divinam operationem, videtur hic dicere, quæ sic actione et contemplatione completur, et quasi eminenter utriusque vim habet : sapientiam scilicet, quæ proxima est ad deificationem. Quomodo et in Christo dictam θεουργίαν Dionysio, quin dicamus, nihil videtur obstare : non quidem quæ unioni prævia intelligatur et ad eam disponens (quod Nestoriani furfuris est), sed illi comes, ad eamque sequens, velut illius ornatus : in qua ipsa nobis idem Christus et auctor exsistat et perfectissimum exemplar ; cum ejus θεουργία, ut Budæo exponitur,
anchorLine: σῆ τρόπον εὗρε τῆς ἀληθοῦς θεουργίας (v). Ὁ δ'
continued: runs on to the next page (ends 'ut Budæo exponitur,')
en: On 'of true theurgy'. By true theurgy he seems here to mean the divine operation, which is fulfilled by action and contemplation together and holds, as it were eminently, the force of both, namely wisdom, which is nearest to deification. How, then, could the theurgy attributed to Christ by Dionysius not be spoken of in the same way? Nothing seems to stand in the way: not a theurgy understood as preceding the union and disposing toward it (which is a Nestorian bran), but one that accompanies the union and follows it, as its adornment, in which the same Christ is both the author and the most perfect exemplar for us; when his theurgy, as Budaeus explains it, [text continues on the next page].

text: pro divina miraculorum potestate et operatione paucis fuerit communicata, nec ipsa defuerit Veteri Testamento : secus vero θεουργία, qua sic ad deificationem provehimur, ejusque per Christum renatis omnibus facultas tribuitur. Ipsa angelorum operatio, qua inferiores illuminant ac perficiunt, Dionysio θεουργία, ac si dicas, divinis dotibus imbuens. Ipse Maximus sequenti capite clare explicat, sic ex ambobus provenientem sapientiam ; in qua statuit salutis nostræ mysterium (θεουργική scilicet) quo sic deitate imbuimur.
anchorLine: (call stands on p-0684: σῆ τρόπον εὗρε τῆς ἀληθοῦς θεουργίας (v).)
en: [continuing the note from the previous page: '... when his theurgy, as Budaeus explains it,'] ... is taken for the divine power and working of miracles, was imparted to few, and was not lacking even in the Old Testament; but theurgy by which we are advanced to deification, and the capacity for which is bestowed through Christ on all the reborn, is otherwise. The very working of the angels, by which the lower illuminate and perfect, is Dionysius's theurgy, as if you were to say 'imbuing with divine gifts'. Maximus himself explains it clearly in the next chapter: wisdom proceeding from both, in which he places the mystery of our salvation (the theurgic, that is) by which we are thus imbued with deity.

text: Δόξαν δὲ βίου. Claritatem reddidi ; Picus, opinionem. At, quid hic vitæ opinio, ut hoc ratio seu scientia illi dicatur ? Ejus vero claritatem esse seu gloriam, res perspicua sit, cum vita, ejus solum exhibitio sit ac manifestatio. Quod enim ratio ad vitam Maximo comparatur ut anima ad corpus, et ut vitam ei præstans, sine qua inane simulacrum sit, εἴδωλον, ejus plane nobilitas et gloria et claritas est, δόξα, non frigidum illud, opinio.
readingNote: the Greek lemma is badly printed in the plate; letters after the first read as Δ?ξαν δὲ β?ο?; written Δόξαν δὲ βίου because the line it cites (δόξαν δὲ βίου) is in the Greek text and the note itself says δόξα
anchorLine: μὲν λόγου, τὸν βίον (x), δόξαν δὲ βίου, τὸν λόγον
en: On 'δόξαν δὲ βίου' (the glory of life). I have rendered 'claritatem' (splendour); Picus has 'opinionem' (opinion). But what is 'opinion of life' here, that reason or knowledge should be so called of it? That its splendour or glory is meant is plain, since life is only the display and manifestation of it. For reason is compared by Maximus to life as the soul to the body, and as the thing that gives it life, without which it would be an empty image (εἴδωλον); so its plain nobility, glory and splendour is δόξα, not that cold thing called opinion.

text: Μετενέγκας πρὸς τὸν νοῦν τοῖς λόγοις τὴν αἴσθησιν. Altissime hic Maximo explicata, mentis in sensum sensusque in mentem vicaria munia. Nempe sensus rationibus in mentem transfertur, ut ipse conjunctione cum illa velut intelligat : mens vero scite miroque artificio rerum figuris ac formis, seu speciebus, sensui innectitur, iisque quasi vinculis ad eum trahitur ; μετεγκλοιώσας quod nempe non intelligat pro hoc statu, nisi conversione ad phantasmata, ut philosophus loquitur ; quorum necessitudine a nativa puræ mentis ac solutæ ingenuitate ad sensus compositionem velut desciscat, illiusque qualitatem induat. Ducta metaphora a canibus, quorum sunt κλ[...] illi et collaria, quibus ad nutum trahentis aguntur, dicuntur et reorum catenæ et vincula.
unreadable: one Greek word after 'quorum sunt' (κλ.. , apparently a plural of the word for dogs' collars/chains) is ill printed; recorded κλ[...]
anchorLine: πρὸς τὸν νοῦν τοῖς λόγοις τὴν αἴσθησιν (y), ἐν δὲ τῷ
en: On 'μετενέγκας πρὸς τὸν νοῦν τοῖς λόγοις τὴν αἴσθησιν'. Maximus explains very profoundly here the reciprocal offices of mind toward sense and sense toward mind. Sense is carried over into the mind by the ratios, so that the mind itself, through union with it, as it were perceives; the mind, with skilful and wonderful art, is bound to sense by the figures and forms, or species, of things, and is drawn to it as by chains. 'Μετεγκλοιώσας' (putting a collar upon) means that the mind in this present state understands only by turning to phantasms, as the philosopher says; by their necessity it falls away, as it were, from the native, pure and unconstrained freedom of the mind to a composition with sense and takes on its quality. The metaphor is drawn from dogs, whose [κλ...] these are, and the collars by which they are led at the will of the one who draws them; the word is also used of the chains and fetters of the guilty.
